Approved findings

Approved evidence · As of 10 Nov 2026

Experts Rise Where LLMs Disagree: Using Cross-Model Disagreement to Target Expert Effort in LLM Codebook Revision for Large-Scale Annotation (2609.26926v1) · paper method: The workflow computes normalized vote entropy from six LLM predictions and a vote-weighted mean per label to prioritize expert attention over 6,595 unlabeled tutoring utterances; label disagreement is explicitly not a measure that any prediction or label is incorrect.

Approved evidence · As of 10 Nov 2026

Experts Rise Where LLMs Disagree: Using Cross-Model Disagreement to Target Expert Effort in LLM Codebook Revision for Large-Scale Annotation (2609.26926v1) · paper method: Each of two experts supplies rationales for 60 selected utterances, yielding 120 rationalized annotations used by GPT 5.6 Sol to revise 24 codebook entries; reported mean Rationale Labeling time is 169.0 minutes per expert, and workflow target-label assignments differ.

Approved evidence · As of 10 Nov 2026

Experts Rise Where LLMs Disagree: Using Cross-Model Disagreement to Target Expert Effort in LLM Codebook Revision for Large-Scale Annotation (2609.26926v1) · paper method: On the same 4,032 held-out expert-consensus utterances, Rationale Labeling yields 64.9% accuracy and 0.658 weighted F1 versus the final expert-only codebook’s 57.8% and 0.583, averaging eight alternative aggregation methods over one temperature-zero run per codebook from each of six models.

cohort9.claim.expertsrise.heldout-result

  • Aggregators reuse the same predictions and are not independent trials; 6.1% multi-label references are reduced to the first recorded label. This is agreement with a chosen reference label, not measured universal semantic correctness.

Approved evidence · As of 10 Nov 2026

Experts Rise Where LLMs Disagree: Using Cross-Model Disagreement to Target Expert Effort in LLM Codebook Revision for Large-Scale Annotation (2609.26926v1) · paper method: The study covers one longitudinal annotation project with two experts, largely fixed labels, unequal workflow exposure/effort and possible carryover; transcript errors were neither corrected nor systematically measured, so it does not isolate the causal effect of input format alone.
